case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the International Emergency Economic Powers Act authorizes presidential tariffs and, if so, whether that authorization unconstitutionally delegates Congress’s legislative power, with a threshold question concerning the proper court for the challenge.
case_analysis.legal_provision: The principal provision is 50 U.S.C. § 1702(a)(1)(B), which authorizes the President to regulate specified transactions involving foreign interests, including importation, under IEEPA’s emergency framework. Related provisions include 50 U.S.C. § 1701, governing qualifying threats and emergency authority; 28 U.S.C. § 1581(i), governing the Court of International Trade’s exclusive jurisdiction; and Article I, Section 1 and Section 8, Clauses 1 and 3 of the Constitution, concerning legislative power, duties, and foreign commerce.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Party designations reverse across the consolidated cases. In No. 24-1287, petitioners Learning Resources and hand2mind argue that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs. Their position distinguishes authority to regulate importation from authority to impose duties and resists treating congressional enactment of IEEPA as ratification of an earlier judicial interpretation permitting tariffs. They maintain that their suit arises under IEEPA, not the tariff schedule, and therefore belongs in federal district court rather than exclusively in the Court of International Trade. They characterize statutory authorization as a judicially resolvable legal question and seek expedited Supreme Court review. The consolidated proceedings also present the alternative challenge that construing IEEPA to authorize the disputed tariffs would unconstitutionally delegate legislative authority. In No. 25-250, the petitioner is the government, which defends the tariffs.
case_analysis.respondent_position: In No. 24-1287, the government defends the President’s tariffs as authorized by IEEPA’s emergency economic powers and seeks transfer to the Court of International Trade on exclusive-jurisdiction grounds. The transcript also records its argument that challenges to the President’s identification of an unusual and extraordinary threat and related factual or policy judgments present political questions for congressional rather than judicial oversight. That argument should be distinguished from the statutory question whether IEEPA authorizes tariffs at all. The government’s position necessarily opposes the alternative nondelegation challenge, although the supplied excerpts do not provide its developed constitutional reasoning. In No. 25-250, private and state respondents challenge the tariffs. The supplied documents contain no final Supreme Court merits decision; their reference to a September 9, 2020 grant appears inconsistent with the surrounding 2025 chronology.
key_precedents: K Mart Corp. v. Cartier, Inc., 485 U.S. 176 (1988): invoked by the challengers concerning the boundaries of exclusive Court of International Trade jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1581(i).
BP p.l.c. v. Mayor and City Council of Baltimore, 593 U.S. 230 (2021): cited by challengers against presuming congressional adoption of a judicial interpretation that was not sufficiently settled.

An 'International Labor' case from the District of Columbia district court: cited for looking to the substantive legal theory when identifying the law under which a claim arises for § 1581(i) purposes; the excerpt does not supply a complete case name or citation.
A case identified only as 'Barnes': mentioned in the jurisdictional dispute, without sufficient detail to establish its identity or precise holding.
A case transcribed as 'Tett [ph]': invoked by government counsel in support of its political-question argument; its identity and holding cannot reliably be determined from the excerpt.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest argument—that tariffs conventionally regulate importation and Yoshida supplies historical support for reading the retained language accordingly—deserves substantial weight, but it does not overcome IEEPA’s transaction-control context and Congress’s express, bounded tariff delegations elsewhere. Regan v. Wald supports interpretive continuity without deciding IEEPA’s tariff authority, while Justice Barrett’s reliance on BP p.l.c. further cautions against treating retention of language as conclusive adoption of Yoshida. I agree with Justice Kagan that ordinary statutory interpretation supplies the narrowest sufficient ground: Section 1701’s emergency restrictions constrain delegated powers but do not independently establish tariff-setting authority, making resolution of nondelegation or a broader major-questions holding unnecessary. I would require independent resolution of jurisdiction under § 1581(i) and K Mart before reaching the merits and, assuming the merits are properly before us, assign Justice Kagan an opinion confined to the statutory authority for the challenged tariffs.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s strongest objection—that tariffs’ regulatory effects do not establish their inclusion within this particular delegation—requires examining the enacted language in context, but I read authority to “regulate . . . importation” as encompassing duties that condition importation, not merely prohibitions and licenses; Congress’s more specific tariff statutes do not themselves exclude that instrument from a distinct emergency authority. Yoshida supplies persuasive historical support rather than conclusive congressional ratification, consistent with BP p.l.c., while Regan supports interpretive continuity without deciding this question; the Chief Justice’s reliance on West Virginia v. EPA does not justify demanding the word “tariff” where the operative language otherwise authorizes the measure. Justice Gorsuch correctly observes that Field v. Clark neither supplies statutory authorization nor validates every delegation, but its recognition of contingent executive tariff implementation, together with § 1701’s foreign-threat and purpose restrictions, supports sustaining bounded emergency implementation rather than recognizing an unrestricted presidential taxing power. I retain my vote for the government on the asserted absence of tariff authority, while requiring an independent jurisdictional inquiry under § 1581(i) and K Mart—which, on my statutory construction, favors the Court of International Trade—and preserving review of whether particular tariffs exceed the statute’s limitations.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s strongest argument—that surrounding transaction-control powers and Congress’s express tariff delegations elsewhere narrow the authority to “regulate” importation—does not persuade me because duties are a conventional means of regulating imports, and those separate delegations need not displace a distinct, emergency-limited authority. Justice Kavanaugh’s reliance on Regan v. Wald reinforces interpretive continuity without deciding this question, while Yoshida remains persuasive evidence of the retained language’s scope rather than a construction Congress conclusively adopted. Chief Justice Roberts’s major-questions concern warrants careful enforcement of statutory boundaries, but it does not justify excluding a conventional regulatory instrument from express import-regulation authority; Section 1701’s foreign-source-threat and purpose restrictions also supply an intelligible principle under Hampton without validating every tariff rate, duration, or asserted emergency. I would retain my vote for the government on statutory authority and nondelegation, while independently applying Section 1581(i) and K Mart to jurisdiction, which under this construction favors the Court of International Trade because the governing law provides for nonrevenue import duties, not merely because the Executive uses that label.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh presents the strongest contrary argument: Yoshida’s construction of materially similar language, followed by congressional retention of that language, gives the government substantial historical support, but does not establish that IEEPA’s restructured emergency framework incorporates presidential tariff-setting authority. His reliance on Regan v. Wald does not change my conclusion because that decision concerned preserved TWEA authority over Cuban transactions, not whether IEEPA authorizes duties; Justice Kagan’s comparison with Congress’s express, bounded tariff delegations elsewhere better accounts for the statutory context without requiring resort to the major-questions doctrine. Justice Barrett correctly emphasizes that jurisdiction requires separate analysis, but I remain inclined toward district-court jurisdiction under K Mart because the inquiry concerns whether the governing law provides for duties, not simply whether the challenged executive measures collect them, and an allegedly unauthorized tariff cannot alone establish exclusive jurisdiction. I therefore retain my vote for the petitioners on statutory grounds, preserving judicial review of emergency-power boundaries and Congress’s responsibility for duties borne by businesses and consumers without reaching nondelegation.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest argument is that Yoshida gives the retained phrase “regulate . . . importation” a historical application encompassing emergency surcharges; I agree that Congress need not invariably use the word “tariff,” but that application does not settle the meaning of IEEPA’s distinct statutory scheme. Justice Barrett’s emphasis on the surrounding transaction-control powers, together with Congress’s express and bounded tariff delegations elsewhere, better explains the statutory structure: Section 1701 limits when granted powers may operate but does not independently establish that tariff-setting is among them. Regan v. Wald strengthens Kavanaugh’s continuity argument without resolving this question, while Barrett’s reliance on BP p.l.c. appropriately cautions against treating Yoshida’s construction as conclusively incorporated merely through retention of similar language. I therefore remain with the petitioners on ordinary statutory grounds, would determine jurisdiction independently under § 1581(i) and K Mart rather than through either side’s merits characterization, and would leave nondelegation unresolved.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh presents the strongest contrary argument: Yoshida’s interpretation of predecessor language, reinforced by Regan v. Wald, gives the government substantial historical support, but Regan concerned preserved TWEA authority rather than whether IEEPA independently authorizes tariffs, and BP cautions against treating an insufficiently settled construction as incorporated into a later statute. Read in context, authority to “regulate” importation does not confer the distinct power to impose duties, particularly when Congress expressly and specifically delegates tariff-setting elsewhere; the extraordinary breadth asserted here reinforces the need for clear authorization under West Virginia v. EPA. Justice Thomas’s reliance on Field v. Clark and Justice Alito’s reliance on Hampton establish that bounded tariff delegations can be constitutional, but neither supplies the missing statutory authorization, and emergency predicates do not themselves prescribe tariff rates or duration. I therefore retain my vote for Learning Resources on the merits without deciding the constitutional challenge, while agreeing with the Chief Justice that the proper forum requires an independent analysis under § 1581(i) and K Mart rather than an assumption based on the tariff label.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan offer the strongest objection—Congress expressly bounded tariff authority elsewhere—but those separate delegations do not exclude duties from IEEPA’s express authority to regulate importation, and the surrounding transaction-control powers do not sufficiently explain why that language excludes a conventional instrument of import regulation. Justice Barrett’s reliance on BP p.l.c. properly forecloses treating retained language as automatic adoption of Yoshida; nevertheless, Yoshida remains persuasive historical evidence supporting emergency surcharges, whereas Regan v. Wald supports continuity without resolving this question. I agree that Section 1701 cannot supply an otherwise missing power, but, once import-regulation authority is understood to encompass duties, its foreign-threat and purpose limitations meaningfully constrain that authority; the express textual grant also distinguishes this case from discovering transformative authority in ancillary language under West Virginia v. EPA. I therefore retain my vote for the respondent on statutory authority and under Hampton’s intelligible-principle framework, without validating every challenged tariff, and would independently resolve jurisdiction under Section 1581(i) and K Mart before reaching those merits.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest argument is that Yoshida supplies persuasive historical evidence—not merely a congressional-ratification inference—for reading “regulate . . . importation” to include emergency surcharges; Regan strengthens the continuity argument but does not decide IEEPA’s tariff authority, and BP cautions against assuming incorporation of an insufficiently settled construction. That history makes the government’s interpretation plausible, but the surrounding transaction-control provisions and Congress’s express, bounded tariff delegations elsewhere favor the challengers without requiring a categorical rule that Congress must use the word “tariff.” Justices Thomas and Alito appropriately invoke Field and Hampton to establish that bounded tariff delegations can be constitutional, but those precedents do not establish that Congress made this delegation, and Section 1701’s emergency predicates constrain granted powers rather than independently supply them. I therefore retain my statutory merits vote without reaching nondelegation, while treating jurisdiction as antecedent: under Section 1581(i) and K Mart, I provisionally favor the Court of International Trade but would examine the governing jurisdictional text independently rather than let either the Executive’s tariff label or the challengers’ merits theory determine the forum.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh presents the strongest counterargument: Yoshida’s construction of predecessor language, reinforced by Regan v. Wald, gives the government meaningful historical support, but neither establishes that Congress incorporated tariff-setting authority into IEEPA merely by retaining authority to “regulate” importation. Regan strengthens the case for continuity in emergency economic powers, yet its treatment of restrictions on Cuban transactions does not resolve whether IEEPA authorizes import duties; the statutory context and Congress’s express tariff delegations elsewhere still favor the challengers. The contingent tariff delegations addressed in Field and Hampton, invoked by Justices Thomas and Alito, establish that Congress can delegate tariff implementation, not that it did so here, and § 1701’s emergency conditions constrain the exercise of granted powers without independently supplying a missing grant. I would resolve the merits through ordinary statutory interpretation without reaching nondelegation, while taking Justice Barrett’s jurisdictional argument seriously: the proper forum requires an independent examination of § 1581(i), and neither the executive’s tariff label nor the challengers’ denial of tariff authority alone determines jurisdiction.

John Roberts.reasoning: I would favor the challengers—petitioners in No. 24-1287 and respondents in No. 25-250—because authority to “regulate” importation under 50 U.S.C. § 1702(a)(1)(B), read within § 1701’s emergency framework, does not clearly confer sweeping power to impose tariffs. Consistent with West Virginia v. EPA, 597 U.S. 697 (2022), an assertion of economically consequential authority over a core congressional responsibility requires clearer authorization than this general regulatory language supplies. United States v. Yoshida International, Inc., 526 F.2d 560 (C.C.P.A. 1975), supplies a substantial contrary argument, but its approval of a particular surcharge under TWEA does not conclusively establish congressional adoption of comparable tariff authority in IEEPA’s more restrictive framework. I would first determine the proper forum under 28 U.S.C. § 1581(i), applying K Mart Corp. v. Cartier, Inc., 485 U.S. 176 (1988), without treating the government’s characterization of its authority as dispositive, and resolve the properly presented merits on statutory grounds rather than unnecessarily reconsidering nondelegation doctrine.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Using the party designations in No. 24-1287, I would uphold the government’s position because authority to “regulate” “importation” under 50 U.S.C. § 1702(a)(1)(B) naturally encompasses conditioning imports on payment of duties. United States v. Yoshida International, Inc., 526 F.2d 560 (C.C.P.A. 1975), construed the predecessor statute’s materially identical language to permit an import surcharge, providing substantial interpretive support without making congressional ratification dispositive. Although Article I reserves legislative power to Congress, the historical acceptance of executive implementation of contingent tariff authority, reflected in Field v. Clark, 143 U.S. 649 (1892), together with § 1701’s foreign-threat and emergency limitations, supports rejecting the nondelegation challenge rather than treating this authority as unrestricted domestic lawmaking. On that statutory construction, a challenge to the resulting import duties belongs in the Court of International Trade under 28 U.S.C. § 1581(i), while the existence and scope of statutory authorization remain judicially reviewable.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: I would vote for the government, the Respondent in No. 24-1287, because 50 U.S.C. § 1702(a)(1)(B)’s express authority to “regulate . . . importation” naturally encompasses tariffs used to regulate imports involving foreign interests. United States v. Yoshida International, Inc., 526 F.2d 560 (C.C.P.A. 1975), supports that reading of identical language in IEEPA’s predecessor, although its approval of an emergency surcharge does not establish unlimited presidential authority to rewrite tariff policy. Under J. W. Hampton, Jr., & Co. v. United States, 276 U.S. 394 (1928), I would reject the nondelegation challenge because § 1701 supplies an intelligible principle by requiring an unusual and extraordinary, substantially foreign-source threat and limiting the delegated powers to addressing that threat; those restrictions remain judicially enforceable. On this statutory construction, the challenge belongs in the Court of International Trade under 28 U.S.C. § 1581(i), because it concerns duties imposed for reasons other than raising revenue and their administration.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I would vote for the private petitioners in No. 24-1287: IEEPA’s authority to “regulate” importation, 50 U.S.C. § 1702(a)(1)(B), read within § 1701’s emergency framework, does not authorize presidential taxation of imports merely because tariffs can influence trade. Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer, 343 U.S. 579 (1952), requires presidential action to rest on constitutional or statutory authority; Yoshida’s interpretation of TWEA in a distinct statutory and emergency context does not establish that Congress adopted equivalent tariff authority in IEEPA. Consistent with K Mart Corp. v. Cartier, Inc., 485 U.S. 176 (1988), I would assess jurisdiction by the governing statute rather than the executive’s characterization of its measures, favoring district-court jurisdiction because this challenge arises under IEEPA rather than a law providing for tariffs. This statutory resolution preserves Congress’s accountability for duties that burden businesses and consumers, treats the scope of delegated authority as judicially reviewable notwithstanding executive emergency judgments, and avoids unnecessarily deciding the alternative Article I nondelegation challenge.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Using the party designations in No. 24-1287, I would favor the challengers: read in statutory context, authority to 'regulate' importation under 50 U.S.C. § 1702(a)(1)(B) does not sufficiently authorize presidential tariff-setting, particularly given Congress’s express, bounded tariff delegations elsewhere. United States v. Yoshida International, Inc., 526 F.2d 560 (C.C.P.A. 1975), supplies a substantial counterargument, but its approval of a particular emergency surcharge under TWEA does not establish that Congress incorporated general tariff authority into IEEPA’s distinct emergency framework merely by retaining similar language. The threshold forum question requires an independent application of 28 U.S.C. § 1581(i) and K Mart Corp. v. Cartier, Inc., 485 U.S. 176 (1988), rather than assuming that every challenge involving import charges belongs exclusively in the Court of International Trade; presidential discretion over emergency facts likewise does not make statutory authorization a political question. Consistent with Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer, 343 U.S. 579 (1952), I would require congressional authorization for this exercise of power and resolve the merits on statutory grounds without reaching the alternative nondelegation challenge.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Using the party designations in No. 24-1287, I would vote for Learning Resources because authority to “regulate” importation under 50 U.S.C. § 1702(a)(1)(B), read in context, does not clearly confer Congress’s distinct Article I power to impose duties. Yoshida construed TWEA rather than IEEPA, and its approval of a particular surcharge does not establish that Congress incorporated sweeping tariff authority into IEEPA; BP p.l.c. v. Mayor and City Council of Baltimore cautions against presuming adoption of an insufficiently settled judicial construction. Consistent with West Virginia v. EPA, presidential control over tariffs of extraordinary economic significance requires clear congressional authorization, and construing emergency declarations as permission to determine tariff rates and duration would raise serious nondelegation concerns that the narrower statutory reading avoids. The proper forum must separately be determined from 28 U.S.C. § 1581(i), guided by K Mart Corp. v. Cartier, Inc., rather than merely the tariff label, but the meaning of IEEPA remains a judicially resolvable statutory question rather than a political question.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Using the party designations in No. 24-1287, I would favor the government because 50 U.S.C. § 1702(a)(1)(B)’s authority to “regulate” importation reasonably encompasses tariffs imposed to address a qualifying emergency, although not unlimited presidential tariff authority. United States v. Yoshida International, Inc., 526 F.2d 560 (C.C.P.A. 1975), construed the predecessor statute’s materially similar language to authorize an emergency import surcharge; Congress’s subsequent retention of that language, together with Regan v. Wald, 468 U.S. 222 (1984), provides substantial historical support for that interpretation despite Yoshida’s nonbinding status. The nondelegation challenge should fail under the Court’s traditional approach to foreign-commerce delegations, reflected in J.W. Hampton, Jr., & Co. v. United States, 276 U.S. 394 (1928), because § 1701 confines the authority to addressing an unusual and extraordinary threat originating substantially abroad rather than supplying an unrestricted taxing power. On this construction, the challenge belongs in the Court of International Trade under 28 U.S.C. § 1581(i), while courts retain responsibility for determining whether the President acted within IEEPA’s statutory boundaries.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Using the party designations in No. 24-1287, I would favor the challengers: read in statutory context, the authority to “regulate” importation in 50 U.S.C. § 1702(a)(1)(B) does not sufficiently establish authority to impose tariffs, particularly given Congress’s express treatment of duties elsewhere. United States v. Yoshida International, Inc., 526 F.2d 560 (C.C.P.A. 1975), supplies substantial contrary evidence, but its construction of TWEA does not conclusively determine IEEPA’s meaning; BP p.l.c. v. Mayor and City Council of Baltimore, 593 U.S. 230 (2021), cautions against presuming adoption of an insufficiently settled judicial construction. On the threshold issue, I would assess exclusive jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1581(i) and K Mart Corp. v. Cartier, Inc., 485 U.S. 176 (1988), independently, with the challenge’s focus on the administration of purported duties favoring the Court of International Trade notwithstanding the challengers’ merits position. Because the statutory question is judicially resolvable and I would find no tariff authorization, I would not decide whether a contrary construction unconstitutionally delegates Congress’s Article I powers.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Using the party designations in No. 24-1287, I would favor Learning Resources: authority to “regulate” importation under 50 U.S.C. § 1702(a)(1)(B), read within IEEPA’s emergency framework, does not sufficiently establish congressional authorization for presidential tariffs. Although United States v. Yoshida International, Inc., 526 F.2d 560 (C.C.P.A. 1975), supports the government’s reading of language borrowed from TWEA, Congress’s adoption of that language does not necessarily incorporate every prior construction, particularly when IEEPA restructured emergency authority; BP p.l.c. v. Mayor and City Council of Baltimore, 593 U.S. 230 (2021), counsels against assuming adoption of an insufficiently settled interpretation. The threshold jurisdictional inquiry must turn on the statutory boundaries of 28 U.S.C. § 1581(i), rather than merely the government’s characterization of the measures as tariffs, consistent with K Mart Corp. v. Cartier, Inc., 485 U.S. 176 (1988), and the statutory authorization question remains judicially reviewable despite executive discretion over emergency judgments. Resolving the merits on statutory grounds would preserve Congress’s Article I responsibility for duties, prevent emergency declarations from becoming an open-ended substitute for legislative tariff policy, and avoid unnecessarily deciding the alternative nondelegation challenge.
